subject: Climate & Environment
title: Blue Carbon Ecosystems
description: A fast breakdown of Blue Carbon Ecosystems for builders.

hook.text: Mangroves, seagrasses, and salt marshes capture carbon up to 40 times faster than forests on land.

buildup.text: This coastal carbon — called blue carbon — gets buried in waterlogged sediments for millennia.

discovery.text: Seagrass meadows alone store 10% of the ocean's carbon despite covering less than 0.2% of the floor.

twist.text: When destroyed, these ecosystems release their stored carbon — turning a sink into a source.

climax.text: Protecting and restoring blue carbon habitats is one of the cheapest climate actions available.

punchline.text: The best carbon vaults on Earth are underwater meadows and muddy mangroves.

quiz.question: What is blue carbon?
options: Carbon captured and stored by coastal marine ecosystems
CO₂ absorbed by the deep ocean
Carbon from burning marine fossil fuels

details.summary: Blue carbon ecosystems include mangroves, seagrass meadows, and salt marshes that capture and store carbon in coastal sediments at rates far exceeding terrestrial forests per unit area. Protecting these habitats is a powerful but underused strategy for climate mitigation.
details.whyItMatters: Blue carbon habitats are being destroyed faster than almost any ecosystem on Earth. Each hectare lost releases centuries of stored carbon and removes a natural coastal defense.
takeaways: Blue carbon habitats store carbon in sediments for millennia
They sequester carbon up to 40 times faster than forests per area
Destruction releases vast stores of ancient carbon

faq.question: What makes blue carbon storage so effective?
faq.answer: Coastal sediments are low in oxygen, preserving organic carbon for thousands of years. The plants continuously add new material above, creating deep carbon-rich layers. When undisturbed, these ecosystems are among the most efficient carbon sinks on Earth.

faq.question: How much blue carbon habitat has been lost?
faq.answer: Globally, about 50 percent of salt marshes, 35 percent of mangroves, and 29 percent of seagrasses have been destroyed. When these habitats are degraded, stored carbon is exposed to oxygen and released as CO2, turning sinks into sources.
